title: Hidden treasure (76–81)
hookLine: follow the one who points out your faults as if showing buried treasure; a solid rock is not shaken by wind

lines: SOMETHING YOU DIDN'T WANT TO HEAR.
cards: A boss says the report missed the point. A friend says you've been short lately. A kid says, “you're on your phone again.”
Being corrected stings, and the quick response is easy to predict: heat in the face, a defense ready on the tongue, maybe a small list of the other person's faults, just in case.
The sixth chapter of the Dhammapada starts somewhere else. It treats the person who corrects you like someone handing over a map to buried gold.

teach.b: The chapter is called pandita, the wise one. Verse seventy-six says: if you find a wise person who shows you what to avoid and corrects you, follow them as you'd follow someone who shows you where treasure is hidden.
It will go better for you, not worse. The commentary tells it about an old man named Radha, so poor that the monks weren't sure he should be ordained.

Sariputta, one of the Buddha's chief disciples, remembered that Radha had once given him a single spoonful of food, and took him on. The story says Radha took every correction gladly, never resenting it, and he thrived.
Verse seventy-seven adds that the wise should admonish and hold others back from harm; the good will love them for it, only the bad won't.
Then verse eighty, a lovely picture of craftsmen: “Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.”
And verse eighty-one: “As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.” Put the two together.
Correction is treasure, and blame and praise are both just wind.
The wise person doesn't need praise to feel steady, and doesn't collapse under blame.

teach.h: BLAME AND PRAISE ARE BOTH WIND.
teach.b: They listen for what's useful, like Radha, and let the rest blow past.
The rock doesn't shake, not because nothing hits it, but because it's rooted deeper than the weather.

how: In Buddhist monastic life, being 'easy to admonish' is counted a virtue, and monks formally invite correction from one another, as at the end of the rains retreat.

o: a traveling merchant who sells spices
the wise one, who welcomes correction
a priest who leads temple ceremonies

games.q: match the pieces of verses seventy-six to eighty-one.
p: not shaken by blame or praise

s: verse seventy-six compares the one who corrects you to someone showing treasure
follow such a person; it will be better, not worse.
in the commentary, Radha resented being corrected
the story says he took every correction gladly.
verse eighty-one says the wise aren't moved by praise, only by blame
they falter not amid blame and praise: both are wind.

games.q: you're Sariputta. a very poor old man wants to become a monk, and the others hesitate. you remember he once gave you a single spoonful of food. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it was only a spoonful.
take him on as your student.
give him food and send him home.
games.why: Sariputta remembered the gift and took him on. Radha took every correction gladly, and thrived.

practice: Bring to mind someone who once corrected you and was right: a teacher, a parent, a coach, a friend who said the hard thing. Remember the sting, then what it gave you, and let a little gratitude come if it wants to.
Then sit heavy and grounded as a rock, and let a word of praise drift by in your mind, then a word of blame: both are wind.

wordCard.voice: Pandita. The wise one, who treats correction like treasure, fashions themselves like a craftsman, and stands like a rock in blame and praise.

orig.note: Pali: wise one, learned one, the title of chapter six.

carryVoice: Your line: the rock doesn't shake. Correction is treasure; praise and blame are wind. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 76–79; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of Radha Thera (verse 76)
